paragraphs: Fluid simulation requires substantial computation because the evolving flow must satisfy mathematical equations. This paper combines a conventional simulation procedure with a learned component to accelerate that work. Although the motivation concerns the broader challenge of fluid simulation, the proposed method specifically solves the incompressible Euler equations.

The method uses standard operator splitting, which divides the simulation calculation into separate operations. Within that procedure, a large sparse linear system must be solved. The authors target this computational task with a convolutional network whose architecture is tailored to the problem. They train the network through an unsupervised learning framework, embedding learned approximation within the established solver procedure.

The authors present real-time simulations in both two and three dimensions and report improvements over recently proposed data-driven methods. They describe the resulting flows as realistic and report good generalization. These findings support the usefulness of learning a demanding component of a numerical simulation: the network contributes speed while the surrounding conventional procedure retains its role in organizing the fluid calculation.
icml-2017-accelerating-eulerian-fluid-si.tldr: A tailored convolutional network accelerates a linear-system solve within a conventional fluid simulator, enabling realistic real-time 2D and 3D results.

paragraphs: This paper studies a two-layer ReLU network trained to reproduce a fixed teacher network with the same architecture. Inputs follow a centered spherical Gaussian distribution. The authors derive an analytical expression for the population gradient, making it possible to examine training behavior through an explicit mathematical formula.

The formula reveals structure in the critical points. Points outside the hyperplane spanned by the teacher weights occur in continuous families rather than as isolated points. For two ReLU units, the analysis also identifies regions within that hyperplane containing no critical points. These results describe different parts of the optimization landscape without assuming independent ReLU activations.

For one ReLU unit, convergence to the teacher weights is guaranteed with probability at least (1−ε)/2 when the random initialization has standard deviation bounded by O(ε/√d). For multiple units, the authors prove a convergence result involving an infinitesimal perturbation of initialization, interpreted as spontaneous symmetry breaking. Simulations support the findings. The conclusions therefore connect initialization and convergence within the stated Gaussian teacher–student setting.
icml-2017-an-analytical-formula-of-popul.tldr: An explicit population-gradient formula reveals critical-point structure and conditional convergence behavior for Gaussian-input ReLU teacher–student networks.

paragraphs: Coordinate descent tackles optimization by updating selected coordinates of the parameter vector. The selection decision matters especially when there are many coordinates: a cheap choice may make limited progress, while a more effective choice can require additional work. This paper proposes a new rule for making that decision in very large optimization problems.

The authors prove that their selection scheme has better efficiency than choosing coordinates uniformly at random. Its efficiency can reach that of steepest coordinate descent, with a potential acceleration of up to n, where n is the number of coordinates. This is an upper extent of the possible gain, rather than a speedup promised for every problem.

A practical attraction is that, in many applications, the scheme can be implemented without extra cost and with computational efficiency close to uniform selection. Experiments on Lasso and Ridge regression show promising improvements consistent with the theory. Together, the results suggest that better coordinate choices can improve optimization progress while preserving the inexpensive updates that make coordinate descent useful.
icml-2017-approximate-steepest-coordinat.tldr: A new coordinate-selection rule provably improves on uniform sampling and can approach steepest coordinate descent efficiency at little practical overhead.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to assign a deep network's prediction to its input features. Such assignments are intended to help people understand which parts of an input contribute to an output. The authors approach the problem by first identifying properties that an attribution method ought to satisfy, rather than judging explanations only by how plausible they appear.

They propose two fundamental axioms, Sensitivity and Implementation Invariance, and show that most known attribution methods do not satisfy them. These requirements guide the development of Integrated Gradients. The method works with the original network without modifying it and needs only a few calls to the standard gradient operator, making the proposed approach straightforward to implement.

The authors apply Integrated Gradients to image models, text models, and a chemistry model. These applications demonstrate uses in debugging networks, extracting rules, and helping users engage with model behavior. The contribution combines a principled way to assess attribution methods with a practical procedure, connecting desired explanation properties to a method that can be applied across different kinds of networks.
icml-2017-axiomatic-attribution-for-deep.tldr: Integrated Gradients uses two attribution axioms to guide a simple method for explaining network predictions through input-feature contributions.

paragraphs: Boosted Fitted Q-Iteration learns an approximation of the optimal action-value function from a fixed dataset of transitions. This function describes the value of actions in reinforcement learning. The method belongs to approximate value iteration, but uses boosting to build its estimate through a sequence of additive corrections.

At each iteration, the algorithm approximates a Bellman residual, which represents a discrepancy in the current value estimate. It sums these approximations across iterations. This additive construction can represent increasingly complex functions even while keeping the function space used for each individual approximation unchanged. The overall model gains expressive capacity through accumulated corrections.

A second stated advantage is that residuals decrease as the estimate approaches the optimal value function, making later regression problems easier. The authors provide a theoretical analysis that includes a finite-sample upper bound on error. They also compare the method empirically with Fitted Q-Iteration across different domains and regression techniques. The abstract establishes the rationale and evaluation approach without asserting a uniform empirical advantage over that comparison method.
icml-2017-boosted-fitted-q-iteration-367.tldr: Boosted Fitted Q-Iteration builds action-value estimates by adding fitted Bellman-residual corrections, with a finite-sample error analysis.

paragraphs: Hierarchical forecasting involves related time series and aggregates formed from subsets of those series. A useful forecast must be accurate at each level while also respecting the relationships between levels. This consistency requirement, called coherence, means that forecasts must add up appropriately throughout the hierarchy.

The paper extends the focus from predicting means to producing predictive distributions. A distribution expresses uncertainty about future outcomes, so the task requires more than making individual point predictions consistent. The proposed algorithm combines information from different hierarchy levels through sparse forecast combination and probabilistic hierarchical aggregation. These components allow forecasts at multiple levels to contribute to the resulting distributions.

The authors evaluate the algorithm on simulated data and large-scale electricity smart meter data. They report consistent performance gains against state-of-the-art methods in those evaluations. The contribution matters where users need both uncertainty estimates and compatible forecasts across aggregation levels: it treats these as connected requirements and uses information distributed across the hierarchy to improve the forecasting process.
icml-2017-coherent-probabilistic-forecas.tldr: The paper produces coherent predictive distributions for hierarchical time series by combining information across aggregation levels.

paragraphs: Sequential prediction problems sometimes come with an oracle that can demonstrate good decisions during training. Plain reinforcement learning does not use this additional guidance. This paper develops AggreVaTeD, an imitation-learning approach that uses training-time oracles while allowing policies to be represented by expressive differentiable models such as deep networks.

The authors introduce two gradient procedures for learning these policies. They apply them to a sequential prediction task and several high-dimensional robotics control problems. The stated benefit is faster and more accurate learning with less training data, achieved by bringing oracle information into the training of flexible neural policies.

The theoretical analysis examines how much data imitation learning can require compared with plain reinforcement learning. It indicates that AggreVaTeD can achieve up to an exponential reduction in sample complexity. That is a possible advantage supported by the analysis, rather than a universal reduction for every task. Together, the theory and results support imitation learning as a potentially more effective strategy when suitable training-time oracle guidance is available.
icml-2017-deeply-aggrevated-differentiab.tldr: AggreVaTeD trains differentiable policies using oracle guidance and can require substantially less data than plain reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: This paper addresses a gap between theoretical guarantees and efficient algorithms in active learning. For general concept classes, the tightest upper and lower bounds described in the abstract depend on a quantity called the splitting index. That parameter provides a way to express the difficulty of a learning problem and the performance that theory allows.

The main contribution is an efficient algorithm that attains the upper bound expressed through the splitting index. This matters because an upper bound and an efficient procedure realizing it are distinct achievements. The result connects the existing theoretical description of achievable performance to an algorithm that can deliver that guarantee.

The authors also report good empirical performance, adding experimental support to the theoretical contribution. The central finding is therefore an alignment between an established bound and efficient algorithm design for general concept classes. The splitting index remains the organizing parameter: the result realizes the associated upper bound, giving that theoretical characterization a concrete algorithmic counterpart.
icml-2017-diameter-based-active-learning.tldr: The paper provides an efficient active-learning algorithm that realizes the established upper bound expressed through the splitting index.

paragraphs: Distributed mean estimation asks how clients can communicate enough information to estimate an average while sending few bits. This paper studies that tradeoff without probabilistic assumptions about the data. The motivation is to reduce communication costs in distributed learning and optimization while controlling the error introduced by compressed messages.

For n clients with d-dimensional data, a basic stochastic-rounding method uses a constant number of bits per dimension per client and has mean squared error Θ(d/n). Applying a structured random rotation before quantization improves the error to O((log d)/n). A better coding strategy reduces it further to O(1/n), removing the dimension dependence from that stated error rate.

The authors show that the latter strategy is minimax optimal up to a constant: for the given communication cost, its worst-case error matches the best achievable level within that factor. They also demonstrate the algorithms in distributed k-means through Lloyd's algorithm and in PCA through power iteration. These applications connect the mean-estimation guarantees to broader computational procedures that repeatedly aggregate distributed information.
icml-2017-distributed-mean-estimation-wi.tldr: Random rotation and improved coding reduce distributed mean-estimation error under limited communication, achieving minimax optimality up to a constant.

paragraphs: Gradients of stochastic computations are often estimated with the likelihood-ratio method. These estimates can have substantial variance, so practical methods use baselines to reduce their noise. This paper asks how close such techniques come to the best estimator available within a common mathematical framework.

The authors develop a framework that contains most common gradient estimators as special cases and naturally yields an optimal estimator. That estimator can itself be interpreted through the likelihood-ratio method, making it a reference for assessing practical alternatives. The derivation uses the interchange of differentiation and integration, together with reparameterization and local marginalization.

The framework also connects likelihood-ratio estimation with the reparameterization trick while retaining support for discrete variables. This connection lets methods often treated separately be analyzed within one formulation. In variational-learning evaluations, the authors compare several baselines with the optimal estimator and find that modern estimators perform close to it. The result provides evidence that the evaluated practical techniques already capture much of the improvement available under this framework.
icml-2017-evaluating-the-variance-of-lik.tldr: A unified gradient-estimation framework derives an optimal reference estimator and finds modern methods perform close to it in variational-learning evaluations.

paragraphs: Distributed learning can be slowed by workers that finish late, known as stragglers, or disrupted by worker failures. This paper addresses those problems for synchronous gradient descent through a coding-theoretic framework. The central task is to organize distributed gradient computation so that slow or failed workers can be tolerated.

The approach combines careful replication of data blocks with coding across gradients. Replication introduces deliberate overlap in the work assigned across the system, while gradient coding organizes the computed information to support tolerance to missing or delayed contributions. The contribution is a structured method for using that redundancy in distributed learning.

The authors implement their schemes in Python using MPI and run them on Amazon EC2. They compare against baseline approaches using running time and generalization error, examining both execution behavior and the quality of the learned result. The abstract establishes failure and straggler tolerance and describes this practical evaluation. Its stated finding is the viability of the coding framework, without specifying a numerical speedup or a particular comparative outcome.
icml-2017-gradient-coding-avoiding-strag.tldr: Gradient coding combines replicated data blocks and coded gradients to tolerate slow or failed workers during synchronous gradient descent.

paragraphs: This paper targets large-scale constrained least-squares problems, where an optimization method must reduce fitting error while respecting restrictions on the solution. Its proposed method, Gradient Projection Iterative Sketch, is a randomized first-order algorithm. The authors also develop an accelerated version, providing two related approaches to the same computational task.

The theoretical contribution is a convergence analysis for both algorithms. Such analysis connects the proposed iterative procedures to their behavior as optimization proceeds. The paper also addresses implementation through a tailored line-search scheme. This gives the method a concrete way to choose update sizes as part of an efficient implementation.

Numerical experiments cover multiple large synthetic and real datasets. The authors report computational efficiency relative to a classical accelerated gradient method and variance-reduced stochastic gradient methods. These comparisons place the proposed algorithms alongside established approaches to large optimization problems. The overall contribution combines algorithm design, convergence theory, and an implementation strategy, with experiments supporting the computational usefulness of the resulting methods for constrained least squares.
icml-2017-gradient-projection-iterative-.tldr: Gradient Projection Iterative Sketch and its accelerated variant combine randomized first-order optimization with convergence guarantees for large constrained least-squares problems.

paragraphs: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo uses Hamiltonian dynamics to construct proposals for a Markov chain sampling procedure. This paper broadens that approach by allowing non-canonical Hamiltonian dynamics. The resulting algorithm, magnetic HMC, explores a larger family of dynamics for proposing moves within Markov chain Monte Carlo.

The name comes from a physical connection: in three dimensions, a subset of the proposed dynamics corresponds to a charged particle interacting with a magnetic field. The authors establish a theoretical basis for using the broader dynamics in MCMC. They also construct a symplectic integrator resembling leapfrog, providing a numerical procedure that makes magnetic HMC implementable.

The paper presents several examples in which the modified dynamics improve mixing relative to ordinary HMC. Better mixing means the sampling process moves more effectively through the distribution being explored. These examples demonstrate that non-canonical dynamics can provide a practical benefit, while the theoretical and numerical developments explain how to incorporate them into a sampling algorithm. The reported advantage is possible and example-dependent, rather than universal.
icml-2017-magnetic-hamiltonian-monte-car.tldr: Magnetic HMC extends Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with non-canonical dynamics and demonstrates improved mixing in several examples.

paragraphs: The paper proposes meProp, a neural-network training technique that keeps the usual forward computation but makes backpropagation sparse. During the backward pass, it uses only a small subset of the full gradient to update parameters. The selection rule keeps the k gradient-vector entries with the largest magnitudes.

This sparsity means that only k rows or columns of a weight matrix are modified, depending on how the matrix is arranged. The stated computational reduction scales with k divided by the gradient-vector dimension. The method therefore connects a simple rule for retaining gradient entries to a direct reduction in the corresponding backward computation.

In the reported experiments, updating only 1–4% of the weights per backward pass did not require more training iterations. The resulting models also achieved improved accuracy rather than an accuracy loss. These are empirical findings about the evaluated training settings. They show that aggressively reducing the information used in each update can save computation while still supporting effective learning, and in these experiments also improved the final predictions.
icml-2017-meprop-sparsified-back-propaga.tldr: meProp retains only large-magnitude gradient entries during backpropagation, reducing computation and improving accuracy in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies how efficiently ReLU networks and rational functions can approximate one another. Rational functions are ratios of polynomials, giving them a different representation from neural networks. The authors show that both representations can approximate the other with a favorable dependence on the requested error tolerance.

For approximation error ε, a ReLU network can be approximated by a rational function whose degree grows as O(polylog(1/ε)). Conversely, a rational function can be approximated by a ReLU network with size O(polylog(1/ε)). Polynomials behave differently: approximating even one ReLU requires degree growing at least as Ω(poly(1/ε)). This comparison highlights the representational advantage of allowing rational functions.

There is an important depth qualification. When converting a network into a rational function, the hidden constants depend exponentially on the number of layers, and the authors show that this dependence is tight. Thus, the favorable dependence on accuracy does not remove the effect of network depth. The result also shows why keeping a compositional representation can be beneficial even when working with rational functions.
icml-2017-neural-networks-and-rational-f.tldr: ReLU networks and rational functions approximate each other efficiently in accuracy, but converting networks incurs an unavoidable exponential dependence on depth.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate mutual information from independent samples of an unknown multivariate distribution. Mutual information describes statistical dependence. Existing approaches face a tradeoff: Gaussian estimators can work in high dimensions when their assumption is correct, but can fail badly when it is wrong.

More flexible nonparametric estimators avoid that narrow distributional assumption, yet the abstract reports that realistic sample sizes are generally insufficient outside very low dimensions. The authors propose a middle ground by assuming a nonparanormal, or Gaussian copula, model. This semiparametric choice lies between a fully Gaussian model and a broad nonparametric class.

The contribution is a set of mutual-information estimators designed for that intermediate model. Theoretical bounds and experiments support a practical balance between robustness and scalability. The approach matters because flexibility and high-dimensional estimation are being addressed together, through a deliberate modeling compromise. Its robustness claim remains tied to the nonparanormal setting; the results do not remove the need for a distributional assumption.
icml-2017-nonparanormal-information-esti.tldr: Nonparanormal mutual-information estimators balance robustness and scalability between restrictive Gaussian models and data-hungry nonparametric approaches.

paragraphs: Ordinal variables are categories with a meaningful order, such as ratings from one to five stars. The paper studies graphical models for collections of these variables. Much earlier work on Markov random fields focused on continuous measurements or unordered categories, leaving the structure of ordinal data less directly addressed.

The authors organize their analysis around two main categories of univariate ordinal distributions and investigate corresponding classes of multivariate graphical models. Extending a model from one ordinal variable to many can create difficulties: earlier constructions may require many parameters or have non-convex likelihoods. Existing tractable approximations also lack strong statistical guarantees and can remain computationally expensive.

The paper develops theory supporting two corresponding classes of estimators that are computationally efficient and have strong statistical guarantees. The significance is the combination of appropriate ordinal modeling, manageable computation, and statistical justification. Rather than treating ordering as an incidental feature of categorical data, the work builds the multivariate models around the two established approaches to describing individual ordinal variables.
icml-2017-ordinal-graphical-models-a-tal.tldr: The paper develops two classes of ordinal graphical-model estimators that combine computational efficiency with strong statistical guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper focuses on learning mixed-membership models when the number of observed variables p greatly exceeds the number of hidden components k. In that setting, tensor methods can become computationally demanding because their intermediate representation scales with the much larger observed-variable count.

The proposed algorithm replaces decomposition of an O(p³)-sized tensor with factorization of O(p/k) smaller tensors, each of size O(k³). This partitioning changes the central computational task from processing one large tensor to handling multiple tensors whose dimensions are governed by the number of hidden components. It directly targets the imbalance between many variables and relatively few components.

The authors also address negative entries in empirical estimators obtained through the method of moments. They provide sufficient conditions for provable guarantees and report competitive results on simulated and real data. The guarantee is therefore conditional on the stated sufficient conditions, while the experiments support practical competitiveness. The main contribution is a more economical tensor-based learning procedure for the regime where p is much larger than k.
icml-2017-partitioned-tensor-factorizati.tldr: Partitioning a large tensor into smaller component-sized tensors reduces the computational burden of learning mixed-membership models under sufficient guarantee conditions.

paragraphs: The paper considers repeated optimization of submodular functions drawn from an unknown distribution. In a recommender system, for example, different users may assign different utilities to sets of items. When the available item collection is enormous, even a commonly used lazy greedy procedure can be too slow.

The authors use training examples of functions to select a smaller ground set of items. New functions from the same distribution are then optimized over that reduced collection, with the aim of retaining nearly the value available from the full collection. They formulate this as a two-stage submodular maximization problem and provide an efficient algorithm.

For general monotone submodular functions under general matroid constraints, the algorithm has approximation ratio (1/2)(1−1/e²). In several real-world applications, optimization on the reduced set runs about two orders of magnitude faster with almost no loss in value. The theoretical ratio and the stronger observed retention describe different evidence: the former is a guarantee for the stated class, while the latter is an empirical result.
icml-2017-probabilistic-submodular-maxim.tldr: Learning a smaller item set makes later submodular optimization much faster while retaining nearly all value in the reported applications.

paragraphs: Fisher information and natural gradients provide geometric tools for understanding and improving neural-network learning. Applying that analysis becomes harder as a model grows larger and more complex. This paper takes a preliminary step toward simplifying the problem by focusing on individual components within a larger neural system.

The authors define a relative Fisher information metric for a selected local component. The metric is designed to describe that component accurately while remaining invariant to the other parts of the system. This local formulation simplifies the geometry that must be analyzed, making the resulting information easier to use in guiding learning.

The paper analyzes a collection of commonly used components and demonstrates how the relative metric can improve optimization. Its contribution is therefore both conceptual and practical: it supplies a component-level object for geometric analysis and shows how that object can influence training. The work is presented as an initial direction for handling large modular models, with demonstrated optimization improvements rather than a claim that all difficulties of full-system analysis are resolved.
icml-2017-relative-fisher-information-an.tldr: Relative Fisher information simplifies geometric analysis of neural-network components and provides a local tool for improving optimization.

paragraphs: Resource allocation for influence, information spread, or coverage depends on parameters that are rarely known precisely. Choosing an allocation using incorrect values can produce undesirable outcomes. This paper studies a continuous budget-allocation problem in which the decision must account explicitly for uncertainty in those parameters.

The robust formulation allows an adversary to choose the least favorable parameters within a confidence set. This creates a saddle-point problem that is nonconvex on one side and concave on the other. The allocation is therefore assessed against adverse parameter choices that remain inside the specified uncertainty set.

The authors show that the resulting nonconvex problem can be solved exactly by exploiting connections to continuous submodular functions. Their approach involves a constrained submodular minimization problem. Although that type of minimization is difficult in general, they establish conditions under which the relevant problem can be solved to arbitrary precision ε. The result identifies mathematical structure that makes robust allocation tractable under those conditions, despite the apparent difficulty of the overall formulation.
icml-2017-robust-budget-allocation-via-c.tldr: Continuous submodular structure enables exact robust budget allocation, with conditions supporting arbitrarily precise constrained minimization.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decisions when each available action has both a cost and a risk. At each round, the learner observes a context, chooses an action, and receives only that action's cost and risk. The objective is to keep total cost low while controlling average accumulated risk relative to a predefined threshold.

The authors first develop a method for a full-information online convex problem, where each round reveals a convex loss and a convex constraint. Their meta-algorithm uses online mirror descent. They then extend it to the contextual-bandit setting with sequential risk constraints by incorporating expert advice.

The algorithms achieve near-optimal cost regret while keeping accumulated risk-constraint violation sublinear. Sublinear growth means the violation grows more slowly than the number of rounds, so its average contribution diminishes. This guarantee allows accumulated violations and does not require every individual action to stay below the risk threshold. A simple simulated robotics reactive-control task supports the theoretical results, illustrating the joint treatment of learning performance and long-run risk control.
icml-2017-safety-aware-algorithms-for-ad.tldr: The proposed contextual-bandit algorithms achieve near-optimal cost regret while keeping accumulated risk-constraint violations sublinear.

paragraphs: High-order interactions capture predictive relationships involving combinations of several variables. Finding statistically significant interactions is difficult because the number of possible combinations can be enormous, exceeding 10¹⁷ in the setting described by the authors. This paper studies both selecting a sparse collection of interactions and performing statistical inference about them.

The main contribution extends a selective-inference framework developed for linear models to high-order interaction models. Selective inference accounts for the event that led particular features to be chosen. The authors develop an algorithm that efficiently characterizes this selection event for high-order interactions, addressing a computational obstacle created by the huge candidate space.

The algorithm is applied to an HIV drug-response prediction problem, where the authors demonstrate its effectiveness. The contribution concerns the connection between model selection and statistical assessment: identifying an interaction for a predictive model and evaluating its significance are linked tasks. By making the relevant selection event tractable to characterize, the method brings selective inference to a setting with exceptionally many possible interactions.
icml-2017-selective-inference-for-sparse.tldr: An efficient selection-event algorithm extends selective inference to sparse models with enormous numbers of possible high-order interactions.

paragraphs: The paper addresses optimization objectives made from a large sum of nonconvex functions plus a regularization term. It develops a stochastic version of the Difference of Convex functions Algorithm, or DCA. The application of interest is selecting groups of variables while training a classifier.

For group selection, the authors use ℓ₂,₀ regularization. They exploit the structure of the objective to construct an efficient difference-of-convex decomposition. The resulting stochastic procedure has inexpensive subproblems: it only requires projections of points onto balls, and those projections can be calculated explicitly. This makes the mathematical decomposition directly relevant to the cost of carrying out the algorithm.

The method is applied to group-variable selection in multiclass logistic regression. Experiments on benchmark and synthetic datasets report advantages over well-known methods in classification accuracy, solution sparsity, and running time. These findings support the approach as a practical way to combine predictive learning and group selection in the evaluated settings. The contribution links a structured nonconvex formulation to simple computations and favorable empirical results.
icml-2017-stochastic-dca-for-the-large-s.tldr: A stochastic difference-of-convex algorithm uses inexpensive explicit projections for group-variable selection and performs favorably in multiclass classification experiments.

paragraphs: Tensor balancing rescales a nonnegative multidimensional array so that every fiber sums to one. For an Nth-order tensor, the rescaling uses N tensors of order N−1. The paper generalizes matrix balancing, a process used to make matrices comparable across applications ranging from biology to economics.

The authors represent tensors as probability distributions on a statistical manifold. In that representation, balancing becomes projection onto a submanifold. This geometric view supports a proof of correctness and an efficient Newton-based algorithm. A key step is obtaining the required Jacobian analytically through the Möbius inversion formula, making the geometric formulation useful for actual computation.

The proposed algorithm has quadratic convergence, and numerical experiments show it running several orders of magnitude faster than existing methods. The authors also describe the underlying model as broader than tensor balancing, encompassing models such as weighted directed acyclic graphs and Boltzmann machines. Thus, the immediate result is a faster balancing procedure, while the probability-based geometric representation offers a framework with wider stated applicability.
icml-2017-tensor-balancing-on-statistica.tldr: A statistical-manifold formulation yields a quadratically convergent Newton algorithm for tensor balancing with substantial experimental speedups.
